title: Top K Frequent Elements
description: Brute force to optimized: sorting every distinct value versus a bounded min heap versus bucket sort by frequency.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequently occurring elements, in any order.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Most Requested Songs on a Playlist
blocks.text: Like tallying how many times each song on a long playlist has been played, and pulling out just the handful of songs requested most often, without needing to fully rank every single song on the list.

blocks.caption: Find the k elements that occur most often in the array

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["1 appears 3 times, 2 appears 2 times, 3 appears 1 time","the top 2 most frequent are 1 and 2","1 and 2 have the two highest frequencies among all distinct values, 3 and 2 respectively"],["Answer","[1, 2]","These are the 2 elements with the highest occurrence counts, in either order"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Only one distinct value exists","it is trivially the most frequent","With no other values to compare against, the single distinct value automatically ranks first"],["Answer","[1]","The only possible choice for the single most frequent element"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: k equal to the number of distinct elements
If k equals the total number of distinct values, the answer is simply every distinct value, in any order.

Before sorting every distinct value by frequency, notice the question only asks for the top k, not a full ranking of every single distinct value, and "only the top k" is a strong hint that a full sort is doing more work than the question actually needs.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Sorting every distinct value by frequency correctly finds the top k, but it fully orders every one of the d distinct values, even though only the k largest ones are ever used.

Observation 2: A heap capped at size k, popping the smallest whenever it exceeds that size, keeps exactly the k largest frequencies seen so far without ever needing the other d minus k values sorted relative to each other.

Observation 3: Frequency itself has a special property this problem's values do not: it can never exceed n, the array's own length, a small, fixed, known range regardless of how large the actual values in nums are.

Observation 4: Since frequency is bounded by n, an array of n plus 1 buckets, one per possible frequency, lets every distinct value be placed directly into its bucket in O(1), and scanning those buckets from highest to lowest frequency reads off the top k values without comparing anything at all.

Whenever a "find the top k by some metric" problem's metric itself is bounded by a small, known range, consider bucket sort by that metric instead of a heap, trading a log factor for direct array indexing.

This problem is a clean progression through 3 genuinely different levels of the same "top k" idea: full sort, bounded heap, and finally frequency-bucketing, each removing a bit more unnecessary work than the last.
Count every value's frequency, then sort every distinct value by its frequency in descending order and take the first k.

items: Count how many times each distinct value appears.
Sort the distinct values by frequency, highest first.
Take the first k values from that sorted order.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: counts is built in a single pass over nums before any sorting begins, since sorting needs each distinct value's total frequency to already be known.
The sort key is the frequency associated with each distinct value, not the frequencies themselves, since the actual values are what the function must return.

Only the first k entries of the fully sorted list are returned, discarding the sorting work already done on the remaining d minus k values, which is exactly the wasted effort the later optimizations target.

blocks.text: Sorting every distinct value by frequency and taking the top k correctly produces the most frequent elements.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d log d), where d is the number of distinct values, dominated by the sort.
Space: O(d), for the counts and the sorted list.
Limitation: sorting every distinct value is more work than necessary when only the top k are actually needed, especially when d is much larger than k.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Full sorting spends effort establishing a total order across every one of the d distinct values, but the question only ever consumes the top k of that order, throwing the rest away. A size-bounded min heap captures this insight directly: it only ever needs to know "is this new candidate better than the worst one currently being kept", a single comparison against the heap's smallest element, rather than a comparison against every other candidate. Popping the smallest whenever the heap exceeds size k guarantees that, at every point, the heap holds the k best candidates seen so far, and by the time every distinct value has been considered, those k candidates are exactly the true global top k, achieved with only O(log k) work per candidate instead of O(log d) for a full sort.

Use a min heap that never grows beyond size k. Push every (frequency, value) pair onto the heap, and whenever the heap size exceeds k, pop the smallest frequency element off. Once every distinct value has been processed, the heap holds exactly the k most frequent values, without ever fully sorting all d of them.
A size-bounded min heap, keeping only the k most frequent elements seen so far.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Heap contents (value: frequency)","Why"],"rows":[["Push 1 (frequency 3)","{1:3}","The heap has room (size 1, cap 2), so the new candidate is simply added"],["Push 2 (frequency 2)","{1:3, 2:2}","The heap still has room (size 2, cap 2), so this candidate is also added directly"],["Push 3 (frequency 1), heap now exceeds size 2, pop the smallest","3 (frequency 1) is popped, leaving {1:3, 2:2}","Adding 3 pushed the heap over its cap of 2, so the currently weakest candidate, 3, the smallest frequency, is evicted"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: a min heap capped at size k, popping the smallest whenever it overflows

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d log k), pushing every distinct value onto a heap capped at size k.
Space: O(d plus k), for the frequency map and the heap.

A min heap capped at size k always exposes its current smallest element at the top, which is exactly the weakest candidate among everything kept so far. Popping that element whenever a new, better candidate arrives and the heap overflows guarantees the heap never holds more than the k strongest candidates seen up to that point, and since every distinct value is eventually considered, the heap converges to holding precisely the true global top k by the end.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Heap state","Meaning"],"rows":[["Size less than k","Every candidate seen so far is automatically kept, since there is no need to evict anything yet"],["Size equal to k after a push","The weakest of the k plus 1 candidates currently held is evicted, keeping only the k strongest"]]}

items: The heap stores frequency first in each pushed pair, since the heap orders elements by their first component, frequency, not the value itself.
The size check and pop run after every single push, immediately trimming the heap back down to size k whenever it briefly grows to k plus 1.
The final result is extracted by reading only the value component out of each remaining pair, discarding the frequency once it has served its purpose of ordering the heap.

No explicit sort is ever applied to the final k elements, since the problem only requires them in any order, and a heap does not maintain a sorted structure beyond guaranteeing quick access to its minimum.

blocks.text: 10. Further Optimization: Bucket Sort by Frequency

Frequency can never exceed the total length of the array, so instead of a heap, create an array of buckets indexed by frequency (0 through n), and place each distinct value into the bucket matching its frequency. Then scan the buckets from the highest frequency down to the lowest, collecting values until k of them have been gathered. This avoids the log factor from the heap entirely.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Scan from bucket 3 down: collect 1 from bucket 3","one value collected"],["Continue to bucket 2: collect 2","two values collected, k reached, stop"],["Answer","[1, 2]"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: bucket values by frequency, scan from the highest bucket down

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), counting frequencies and bucketing in linear passes, with no sorting or heap operations at all.
Space: O(n), for the buckets array.

items: The buckets array allocates exactly one bucket per possible frequency value, from 0 up to the maximum possible frequency of n, every element being the same value.
Each distinct value is placed directly into the bucket matching its own frequency, an O(1) operation per distinct value with no comparisons at all.
The final scan runs from the highest possible frequency index down to 1, skipping bucket 0 entirely, since a value's frequency is always at least 1 for it to have appeared in nums in the first place.
The scan stops the instant k values have been collected, avoiding any unnecessary work scanning through lower-frequency buckets once the answer is already complete.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (full sort by frequency)","O(d log d)","O(d)","d is the number of distinct values; every one of them is fully ordered even though only k are needed"],["Optimized (bounded min heap)","O(d log k)","O(d plus k)","Only a size-k heap is maintained; each of the d candidates costs O(log k) instead of O(log d)"],["Further optimized (bucket sort by frequency)","O(n)","O(n)","No comparisons at all; frequency's bounded range (0 to n) allows direct bucket placement and a single scan"]]}

blocks.text: Bucket sort by frequency works here because frequency is bounded by the array length, a much smaller and more structured range than the values themselves, letting the "sort by frequency" step be done in linear time instead of using a heap or comparison sort.

items: Forgetting that a min heap capped at size k keeps the least frequent of the top candidates at the top, which is exactly what should be popped when the heap overflows, not the most frequent, a natural but incorrect instinct.
Sorting the entire bucket array by index instead of simply scanning it directly from the highest index down, which is already naturally ordered by frequency and needs no additional sorting.
Forgetting to stop the bucket scan the moment k values have been collected, which would waste time continuing to scan through the remaining lower-frequency buckets unnecessarily.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["k equal to the total number of distinct values","The scan naturally collects every one of them, since it only stops early once k is reached, which happens to be everything here"],["Many values sharing the exact same frequency","The bucket approach handles this naturally by grouping them together in the same bucket, with no special handling needed"]]}

items: Present the heap approach first since it directly demonstrates the "top k" pattern in a widely applicable form, then offer bucket sort as the further optimization once the frequency-is-bounded-by-n insight is recognized.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the top k, k most frequent, or k largest, without needing everything else ranked" points toward a size-bounded heap first, since it is widely applicable, then checking whether the ranking metric itself has a small bounded range that would let bucket sort remove the log factor entirely.

items: How would you solve this if k could change between repeated queries on the same array? Precompute the frequency counts once, and either keep the full bucket array around to re-scan per query, or maintain a persistent sorted structure if queries happen very frequently.

What if the array were a live, continuously updating stream? A heap-based approach adapts more naturally to a stream than bucket sort, since frequencies, and thus bucket assignments, would otherwise need constant re-bucketing as counts change.

How would Top K Frequent Words differ from this problem? The same bucket-by-frequency idea applies, but ties in frequency must then be broken by a secondary rule, such as alphabetical order, requiring each bucket's contents to also be sorted or compared on that secondary key.
Classic "top-k" pattern also seen in K Closest Points to Origin and Kth Largest Element, all solvable with the same size-bounded heap technique.
Same "the ranking metric itself has a small bounded range, so bucket by it directly" insight as counting sort and radix sort style optimizations over comparison-based sorting.
Same hash map frequency counting foundation as Ransom Note, Contains Duplicate, and Longest Consecutive Sequence, just paired here with a top-k selection step on top.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force (full sort): O(d log d) time, O(d) space.
Optimized (bounded min heap): O(d log k) time, O(d plus k) space.
Further optimized (bucket sort by frequency): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Frequency counting combined with top-k selection, refined from full sort to a bounded heap to bucket sort
Core Idea: Since frequency is bounded by the array's own length, bucketing distinct values by frequency and scanning from the highest bucket down avoids comparisons entirely
Time: O(n) for the bucket sort version, O(d log k) for the heap version
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: When a "find the top k" problem's ranking metric has a small, known bounded range, bucket sort by that metric beats both a full sort and a heap
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Frequency can't exceed n, so bucket by frequency and read off the top from the top bucket down
